draft:
Choice screens are not market choice

A choice screen can offer you six search engines and still leave you with no meaningful choice. The contradiction is easy to miss because the screen looks like a tiny ballot: several names, one click, a reassuring promise that the market has arrived. But who put those names on the ballot, and who decided what counted as an acceptable answer?

The answer is usually the gatekeeper – a platform, operating system, browser, app store, or marketplace selects the available options before you see them. It defines the category, sets the terms of entry, and controls the machinery through which the decision becomes real. You are choosing inside someone else’s room, from objects someone else has carried there.

That doesn’t make every choice screen fraudulent. Sometimes a curated list is useful (nobody wants to configure a network stack before breakfast). The problem begins when curation is presented as competition. If the gatekeeper chooses the contestants, controls their visibility, and owns the switch that can remove them, the screen is a stage set. The scenery changes; the power doesn’t.

Defaults do even more work than the list itself. A default is the option you get when you do nothing, and doing nothing is a perfectly rational response to friction. You may be busy, uncertain, or simply unaware that a decision has been made on your behalf. The default becomes the path of least resistance, which means the person who sets it is shaping behaviour without having to persuade anyone.

We’ve all seen this in permission dialogs, subscription renewals, telemetry settings, and software installation. A box is already checked. A button is brighter. One route preserves the existing configuration while another asks you to learn a new system. You can technically choose, but the interface has already spent its influence before you arrive. That’s choice in the same sense that a revolving door is an invitation to leave: the exit exists, but the building still determines where you walk.

I don’t mean that users are helpless. I mean that the burden has been placed in the wrong hands. When you must inspect every menu, compare every provider, and undo a preset decision before you can exercise control, the market is charging you in attention. You’ve been given a menu, not power over the kitchen.

A defender of these screens might call them “neutral.” That’s a useful slogan, because it sounds modest while hiding the machinery underneath. Neutral compared with what? A blank page, or a system in which providers can reach users on equal terms? If the gatekeeper chooses the list and the default, neutrality is bullshit. It is a description of the paint, not the architecture.

Here is the distinction we need: nominal choice asks whether an alternative is visible; meaningful choice asks whether the user can reach it on fair terms. I’d look for several concrete conditions. You should be able to install, remove, or replace a service without losing unrelated functionality. Providers should be able to compete for inclusion through transparent rules, rather than through private access to the gatekeeper. The default should be reversible, clearly explained, and easy to change. You should also be able to take your data and relationships with you when you leave.

Those conditions change the structure of the transaction. They make the platform less like a shopkeeper who selects every product and more like a market square with open entrances (the owner can still maintain the pavement). We’re still dealing with an institution, not a magical zone without rules. But our options are no longer limited to the items it has approved, and our exit no longer requires us to abandon the parts of our digital lives that the gatekeeper has bundled together.

I’ve come to distrust the word “choice” when it appears without a description of who controls the menu. I’m not asking for infinite options or an interface that dumps every technical decision onto you. I’m asking for a remedy aimed at power: open access, portable data, contestable defaults, and rules that prevent one company from deciding which alternatives can exist in practice.

We can keep the screen. We can keep helpful recommendations. What we can’t keep is the claim that a list, by itself, transfers control. A choice screen is meaningful only when you can act beyond the gatekeeper’s preferred path, and when leaving doesn’t mean losing the world you built inside it. That is market choice.
